title: Basic quiz: C
prompt: The C that the assembly lessons start from: type sizes, integer division, copies against addresses, where an array element sits, `printf` specifiers, and where a call's arguments go.

questions.question: How many bytes does a long take on the 64-bit ARM Linux machines this site imitates?
questions.explanation: A long is 8 bytes, 64 bits, the size of an x register. An int is 4 bytes, a short 2 and a char 1, which is why assembly has a load and a store for each size.
questions.hint: It fills a whole x register.

questions.question: Both values are int. What is -17 / 5 in C?
questions.explanation: Division of two ints drops the fraction and cuts toward zero, so -3.4 becomes -3, not -4. The remainder, -17 % 5, is -2, because 5 * -3 + (-2) = -17. sdiv in assembly cuts the same way.
questions.hint: The fraction is thrown away, and the result moves toward zero.

questions.question: void bump(int x) { x = x + 1; } is called as bump(score). What happens to score?
options: It goes up by 1, because x is score
It keeps its value, because x is a copy
It becomes 0, because x is never returned
The call does not compile without a return
questions.explanation: C passes arguments by value, so x is a new variable that starts as a copy of score. Adding 1 to x changes only the copy, so score keeps its value. To change score, the caller passes &score and the function writes through the pointer.
questions.hint: The function gets a copy of each argument.

questions.question: int marks[6] starts at address 2000. At which address does marks[3] start?
questions.explanation: Each int takes 4 bytes, so element i starts 4 * i bytes past the start of the array. marks[3] is 12 bytes in, at 2012. In assembly the same sum appears as the SXTW 2 in a load, which multiplies the index by 4.
questions.hint: Multiply the index by the size of one element.

questions.question: Which printf specifier prints an int in hexadecimal?
questions.explanation: %x prints an integer in base 16, so printf("%x", 255) prints ff. %d prints in decimal, %c prints one character, and %s prints a string.

questions.question: int *p = marks; is followed by *p = 0;. What does the second line change?
options: the pointer p, which now holds the address 0
every element of marks, which all become 0
nothing, because p holds a copy of the array
marks[0], the element p points at
questions.explanation: An array's name on its own is the address of its first element, so p holds the address of marks[0]. *p means the value at that address, so *p = 0 stores 0 into marks[0] and changes nothing else.
questions.hint: A * in front of a pointer means the value stored at its address.

questions.question: C calls average3(s1, s2, s3), and all three are int. In the assembly, where do the three arguments travel?
options: On the stack, pushed from right to left
In w0, w1 and w2, in that order
In x19, x20 and x21, the saved registers
In the .data section, beside the strings
questions.explanation: The first eight integer arguments travel in registers, starting at w0 (x0 for a long or a pointer), and the answer comes back in w0. The stack carries only the arguments past the eighth.
questions.hint: Look at the mov lines just before the bl in an assembly call.
